name: /Xam
confidence_why: Known only second-hand: Meriggi 1928 reports the tone system after another work; the primary description was not read.
catalog_citation: Meriggi, Piero. 1928/29. Versuch einer Grammatik des /Xam-Buschmännischen. Zeitschrift für Eingeborenen-Sprachen 19: 117-153, 188-205. Berlin: D. Reimer.

sweep_summary: /Xam (xamm1241, Tuu, extinct) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Schmidt 1986 'Tales and beliefs about eyes-on-his-feet', is a Khoisan folklore chapter (Glottolog record read; the hit is the word 'feet' in a tale-character's name) and is irrelevant. No first-hand statement of /Xam word-stress placement was found in any open source: Bleek & Lloyd 1911 (preface pp. viii-ix) and D.F. Bleek 1956 (note under 'a') speak only of tone marks and 'variations in tone and length'; Bleek 1862's accent section covers Hottentot/Bantu only; Müller 1888's /Kham sketch has no Betonung paragraph; the Tumʔi descriptions (Kilian 2020/2022) say only that schwa is an 'unstressed central vowel' found in non-initial syllables. The likeliest deciding sources remain unread: D.F. Bleek 1928-30 'Bushman grammar' and Meriggi 1928-29 (both in ZES 19, HathiTrust full-view but could not be reached by automated download; not on archive.org), Traill 1995 (print only, Harvard offsite), and Güldemann's |Xam sections in Vossen 2013 'Phonetics and phonology' (doi 10.4324/9780203084465-12) and 'Tonology' (-13), paywalled. Acquisition priority high for all four. ( updated).org worked.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (no catalog record, no statement held by the project). Compatible with D. Bleek 1929:86 (work 1: accent generally on the first syllable): Meriggi gives no placement of his own, adds the classification as a tone language and the caution that the accent diacritics in the Bleek & Lloyd texts partly mark pitch rather than stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Meriggi, working only from the Bleek & Lloyd printed texts plus D. Bleek's letters, classes /Xam ('Buschmännisch') as a tone language with (per D. Bleek) few high and low tones in the southern dialect; the Lautlehre has sections on tone, vowels, consonants, clicks, word shapes, sandhi and spelling variation but NO section on word stress and no statement of where stress falls. Stress ('Stärkeakzent', 'Akzent') is mentioned only in passing: the acute/grave marks of the texts are taken to be accent marks that sometimes encode pitch instead (I §3 Anm. 3; III §10 on the pronouns hì 'us' vs. hí/há), and a possible 'shift of the accent' is invoked for one plural alternation (II §9).
new_statements.exceptions: none (no placement rule given); notes that homophonous stems may be kept apart by pitch (II §7 fn., p.137) and that emphatic ('emphatisch betonten') personal pronouns serve as demonstratives (III §27, p.192: sentence emphasis, not word stress).
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe the /Xam of the Bleek & Lloyd corpus: /xam-ka-!k'e speakers from the northern Cape Colony south of the Orange River recorded 1870-1880 (Bleek 1929 grammar p.81; Comparative vocabularies S1 p.1); Meriggi analyses the printed Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911) texts of the same '/χam' dialect and explicitly sets the !kun (ǃXun) material aside. Bleek phrases her rules for 'Bushman' but every example is /Xam.

new_statements.quote: p.85: 'Tones. Bushman words may vary in meaning according to the tone in which they are spoken. There are three tones to be distinguished, high, middle and low. The middle tone I leave unmarked. The high tone is indicated by placing ¯ before a syllable, the low tone by placing _ before it.' | p.86: 'The accent in Bushman is generally on the first syllable, always if the syllable has a click. The few cases of accentuated second syllables I mark with an accent ´. This occurs most frequently in reduplications.' | p.87: 'Words of one syllable are in the majority. Some words of two syllables are reduplications or compound words, but not all; a number are formed of root and endings.'

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (language not in the catalog, no statement held by the project). First placement statement for xamm1241: initial accent (click-initial syllables always), lexical exceptions on the second syllable mainly in reduplications, coexisting with three lexical level tones. Meriggi 1928/29 (work 0) is compatible (tone language; no placement) and D. Bleek 1929 Comparative vocabularies (work 2) only gives the marking conventions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: /Xam ('Bushman', but the sketch treats only the /xam-ka-!k'e south of the Orange River, p.81) has three level tones (high, mid, low) that can distinguish word meanings, and a word accent that generally falls on the first syllable, obligatorily so when that syllable begins with a click; the few words accented on the second syllable (mostly reduplications) are marked with an acute in her transcription. Most words are monosyllabic; disyllables are reduplications, compounds or root+ending.
new_statements.exceptions: 'The few cases of accentuated second syllables I mark with an accent ´. This occurs most frequently in reduplications.' Tone is also used 'descriptively to denote quantity or distance' (higher tone = larger/farther), p.86.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe the /Xam of the Bleek & Lloyd corpus: /xam-ka-!k'e speakers from the northern Cape Colony south of the Orange River recorded 1870-1880 (Bleek 1929 grammar p.81; Comparative vocabularies S1 p.1); Meriggi analyses the printed Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911) texts of the same '/χam' dialect and explicitly sets the !kun (ǃXun) material aside. new_statements.rule_in_words: A comparative wordlist of 12 doculects (S1 = |kam-ka !ke = /Xam). Its only prosodic content is the transcription key shared by all languages: an acute over a letter marks an accentuated syllable, and words carry high/mid/low (rarely rising/falling) tone marked by dashes; no statement of where the accent falls in /Xam or any other language, and the word 'stress' does not occur in the Introduction.

tone_statements.citation: Meriggi, Piero. 1928-1929. Versuch einer Grammatik des |Xam-Buschmännischen. Zeitschrift für Eingeborenen-Sprachen 19: 117-153, 188-205.
tone_statements.quote: § 1. Buschminnisch gohdrt zu don ,Tonhihensprachen*, a,b, Sprachon, welche sonst véllig gleiche Wérter in verschiedenen Bedoutungen durch verschiedone Tonhihon baw. -bewegungon unter- scheiden. … Uber Tonhihon im Buschm. erfahron wir aus unsoren Toxten wonig. … D. Bl. brioflich folgendes bemerkt: ,Sidbuschmtanisch, wie 2. B. die /zam-Spracho, hat im Vergleich wonige hoho und tiofe Téne. Nordbuschmiinnisch, wie /kwi, hat viel mehr. … § 2. Nach D. Blooks brioflichen Mitteilungon wire allerdings fiir den Tiefton ein hiufiges Zoichen in der Gestalt eines Hakens , unter dem Vokal gebraucht
tone_statements.translation: Par. 1. Bushman belongs to the 'pitch (tone) languages', i.e. languages which distinguish otherwise wholly identical words of different meanings by different pitches or pitch movements. ... About pitches in Bushman we learn little from our texts. ... D. Bl[eek] remarks by letter as follows: 'Southern Bushman, e.g. the /Xam language, has comparatively few high and low tones. Northern Bushman, such as !Kung, has many more.' ... Par. 2. According to D. Bleek's communications by letter, however, a frequent sign for the low tone, in the shape of a hook under the vowel, is used
tone_statements.locator: p. 120, Lautlehre Kap. I par. 1-2 'Tonhoehen' (par. 3 continues on p. 121)

tone_statements.citation: Bertin, G. 1886. Art. III.—The Bushmen and their language. Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland (n.s.) 18(1): 51-81.
tone_statements.quote: It has been objected that Hottentot, which has clicks, has tones also ; but the clicks are probably of Bushman origin, and have been no doubt adopted by the Hottentots in their contact with the Bushmen, as these curious sounds are strangely contagious ; [...] The existence of the clicks is not besides incompatible with that of the tones in the same language, as the former seems to indicate a modification of the beginning, and the latter of the end of the words. However, the existence of tones in the language of the Bushman is even doubtful, as Bleek and others do not mention them.

sources.quote: Finally, the phoneme /ə/ is articulated as an unstressed central vowel. The schwa in Tumʔi generally appears in the second or final syllable, only observed in the first syllable of [|qəri] honey beer, [pəri] 'goat', [məkəs] 'upper thighs', and Afrikaans loan words such as [vələ] 'wild' from the Afrikaans word 'wilde' (vəldə).
sources.locator: 2022 p. 118 (sect. on vowels); same wording in 2020 thesis ch. 3
sources.note: Sections 4-5 cover clicks, consonants, vowels, phonation; no suprasegmental/tone/stress section. Only mention: 'the phoneme /ə/ is articulated as an unstressed central vowel' (p. 118). Describes Tumʔi (Prieska), not 19th-c. |Xam.

sources.quote: It has been objected that Hottentot, which has clicks, has tones also ; but the clicks are probably of Bushman origin, and have been no doubt adopted by the Hottentots in their contact with the Bushmen, as these curious sounds are strangely contagious ; [...] The existence of the clicks is not besides incompatible with that of the tones in the same language, as the former seems to indicate a modification of the beginning, and the latter of the end of the words. However, the existence of tones in the language of the Bushman is even doubtful, as Bleek and others do not mention them.
sources.note: Discusses whether Bushman has tones at all: reports Norris's idea that clicks 'play the same part as the tones in Chinese', notes that Hottentot has both clicks and tones, and concludes that 'the existence of tones in the language of the Bushman is even doubtful, as Bleek and others do not mention them' (p. 64). A pre-Lloyd/D. Bleek second-hand denial, superseded by D. Bleek 1928-30 (three level tones) already listed here.
